review_text_raw:
Great idea, but bad execution. A for effort but C on the result.

PROS:
- Technical polish. The UI looks good and the videos, picture and audio are of good quality.
- The developers did seem to put their heart into this. It is not easy to make games involving so much detail, actors and voice work
- Interesting concept. While not original, piercing the story together through different apps on the phone was neat
- Some puzzles were neat like finding a phone number hidden in Twitter posts or creating a specific Tinder profile, because they fit the concept of the game really well

CONS:
- All the characters are downright unlikable.. I didn't care for Anna one bit and if there was an ending to kill them all off I would have took it. And when I mean all, I really mean all. Every single one, including her mother and the HR lady. I guess only the cat gets a pass and even then I'm not sure
- Unrealistic voice work. Most characters speak very unnaturally. The biggest offender being Greg who talks like he is in a kid's anime
- You can only speak to people when they are online, but they always pop up immediately when you need them to make progress, making it very obvious you are playing a videogame. A few seconds delay would have done wonders for the immersion
- Repetitive gameplay. Most of the time you will be doing the same "construct a phrase" or "remake a picture" puzzle and the whole cycle of restoring the phone data should have only happened once.
- Cheap cheap "horror" with zero atmosphere but instead lots of dumb jump-scares (really really a lot) and in-your-face weirdness. No subtlety whatsoever, making the "horror" cheap, pointless and braindead
- The ending. I felt dumber after the villain reveal and finished the game. Not sure I can put up with another run to see the other endings. I was expecting something stupid, but this worse than I expected

They really should have either cut the "horror" and gone full psychological crime thriller (which would have worked really well with the gameplay) or just go full ham and make the weirdness go on through the whole experience escalating more and more.
Instead you get a detective story ruined by awful jump scares or a horror story bogged down by boring detectice work. I would prefer the former as the later was really really bad, inspired by the worst horror movies the '10s had to offer.

I can forgive the bad dialogues and bad acting due to being an indie game, but I would suggest the developers to at least not use outdated memes in people's speech.

Only buy it on sale and expect a mediocre experience that pisses you off because it had the potential to be much better.

You might think that this is a real-life mystery-horror thriller but no, you will find out that it is a B film in disguise - nonsensical plot, cringy acting, annoying jumpscares, and clichéd ending in one package!

The game was quite intriguing in the beginning. We have to use someone's phone to find out what happened to its owner. To my disappointment, the game got downhill fast.

Puzzles were OK, but watching the video messages was painful. If the devs didn't have enough fundings to hire good actors, then why not just leave out the video? They don't contribute to the plot anyway. There were also jumpscares, which were so out of place and annoying, all sense of immersion I had was ruined by them.

[spoiler]The worst was the ending. The villain was revealed to be an AI called Simulacra, who wanted to kill Anna because, in Simulacra's own words, she "is a worm in a perfect image that needs to be eradicated". Was this line supposed to be scary? Why does Simulacra speak like a cartoon villain?

The ending left me with more questions than answers. The biggest question is: How does an entity that only exists in the virtual space hijack people's bodies in real life?!?!?! Is there a Wi-Fi receiver in the human brain!? 

Even the story premise falls apart when you think about it: 
WHY did the villain/sockpuppet leave the phone on the player's doorstep in the first place?
If Simulacra could imitate other people in the cyberspace, then it could have just destroyed the phone and used Anna's identity to lure more victims online (indeed, at one point in the game Simulacra successfully wiped the phone data), instead of letting the player find out about Anna, who might then rescue her, or worse, warn everyone in the world about the existence of a cyberspace killer. On the topic of warning people, why didn't people who knew Anna contact the police instead of trying to solve the case on their own? When even an ordinary person realised that something fishy was going on, how come the police knew nothing about the disappearances when all the missing people had interacted with each other before they went missing? Did they not bother to do basic investigations?[/spoiler]

Finally, as a VN, being unable to manually save is unacceptable. You have to replay the game from the beginning to get an alternative ending.

It's a shame as this game had great potential to educate people about phone addiction and danger of social media.

Playable, but not to my tastes.

Simulacra is a simple investigative game that requires patience not for the investigation itself, but for its unnatural writing (very clearly non-native English) and its amateurish acted scenes. Jokes dropped like lead balloons, tension dissipated, and what should have been an exciting climax was simply uncomfortable.

The puzzles themselves were relatively entertaining - flicking between apps to piece together information - but the game's "OS" seemed almost incapable of multitasking, and switching between tabs would typically lose form entry data, making the process far more tedious than it should have been.

The game encourages the player to play through multiple times (with a fast-dialogue option after completion), but one playthrough felt like a slog, so I'm unlikely to sit through it again. If you happen to have it in your Steam library, give it a shot, but don't get your hopes too high.

SIMULACRA is a game I first saw on YouTube. I said to myself "Hey, I think I'll pick this up and give it a go. It looks good". Now, after buying it and actually playing it... I just cannot recommend it at all. It feels HEAVILY falsely advertised, to me at least due to the second trailer on steam.  Below I will state why these are my thoughts and what drove me to this conclusion.

[h1][b] My thoughts - Cons? [/b][/h1] 
⚫So to start off, the SECOND steam "TRAILER" for this game has really nothing to do with the game. You get no actual scenes like that at all. Yeah, ok... you get S O M E video scenes but it does NOT look like the second trailer in the slightest and it does not say ANYWHERE "Not actual game footage". 
⚫The game is classed as a "Horror/psychological horror" but as you play it... there is NOTHING scary about the game at all. Do not get me wrong, it had a REALLY great start to it but as you play the game gets overshadowed by "relationship issues" and it takes ALL the horror elements out of the game completely. The more in depth you go the more GOOFIER the plot actually is. Greg with his "Fu** you soooooo much" line or even the sarcastic "Sex offender" you have to talk to that CLEARLY shows who he is. Yeah... nothing mid-end of the game was good at all. 
⚫The lack-there-off accessibility options to turn down audio, adjust frames, settings in general, brightness e.t.c is non existent. You are supposed to be on a phone... come on where is the cog wheel to keep us immersed in this like a REAL phone.

[h1][b] My Verdict [/b][/h1] 
I think that there was to much HYPE based around this game due to several BIG streamers playing it (not going to mention names) and it took off as a "good horror experience" because of it. The lack of horror, accessibility options and sublime goofy plot makes this a dull, boring experience that will leave you feeling like this -  "What did I just spend my time playing" "Was it worth it" "Can I get a refund". 

[h1][b] 3/10 - A goofy plot leads to bad horror experience. [/b][/h1]

I really love this game genre, but this specific game wasn't very good in my opinion, for the following reasons:
- Inconsistent plot. The game just makes use of random horror movie tropes, without them making sense in the story.
- Very cringey characters (both due to the bad writing and to the bad acting), ESPECIALLY the two most important characters in the game: the girl you're supposed to find and the ultimate bad guy. That's a real problem, because it makes it very hard to emphatize with the person you're supposed to save, as well as to take the bad guy seriously.
- Random jumpscares make this game feel pretty shallow.
- Very, very often, the choices that are proposed to you seem forced. Basically, you can feel that the game WANTS the story to progress in a specific direction, and doesn't allow you to very simply avoid issues by being reasonable. For example, at some point, you can either tell a very dangerous lie or tell the truth. But if you tell the truth, at no point does the game allow to explain yourself, and therefore the person you told the truth to just reacts badly for no reason. In real life it would have been easy to avoid that issue, but the game doesn't want that. Hence, choices aren't well made, and overall it doesn't feel like you're really making story progress - it actually more feels like you're following the story where it wants you to go.

Still, there also are some good things:
- The phone interface looks pretty realistic, which is at least one immersive thing
- One playthrough is reasonably long (about 4 hours for the first one), especially since the game is very cheap, and there apparently are four different endings. 
- One or two moments in the story were actually pretty interesting, even though they didn't make sense in the grand scheme of things

Overall, I advice against buying this game, as there are many better ones in the same genre; I for example enjoyed Orwell much more, and both its mechanics and thematics are somewhat similar (without the horror movie aspect of it, which is good riddance honestly), but the writing is much better and realistic (and therefore more immersive as well !) and never made me cringe. Still, Simulacra is very cheap, so if you're okay with what I said above, go ahead.

I want to be kind to this game and for the right person, I would still recommend it. But I don't think SIMULACRA quite pulls it all off. I like the social media sleuth type games (e.g. A Normal Lost Phone.) And the horror twist on this one isn't even that bad if you don't mind breaking the whole simulationist vibe of it.

But there's quality issues. Acting and voiceover ranges from straight-faced to hammy and cartoony and it's not really clear which flavor is intended. There's also *a lot* of spelling and grammar errors that kind of break the sense of immersion. And worst of all, advancing the plot in many cases requires taking actions that the player might have a very good reason not to perform. If I suspect a character of harming the owner of this phone, why should I tell them everything I dig up from social media? Make it make sense.

tl;dr if you want a phone snooping game that is better than this (harder puzzles, better writing) + touches on some of the same themes, and don't mind it being non-horror, try out [b]Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story[/b].

I really like the conceit of a fake computer or phone as the setting for a mystery game, which is why a friend recommended I play this. However, I can't say that I would do the same.

The writing is riddled with typos and unnatural grammatical errors. Like, a lot of these characters aren't even convincingly fluent English speakers. (Also the way their only Black character is written is. reductive.) But it does have its moments that feel natural and compelling.

The acting is... bad. They sound like they're reading off a teleprompter one word at a time, rather than speaking a sentence, and the emotional reactions are not convincing. Worst of the bunch is, unfortunately, one of the two guys whose voice you hear the most. [spoiler](By which I mean Greg.)[/spoiler]

The characterization is weird? IDK, you spend most of your time talking to various brands of Men Who Are Creepy To Women, and it keeps asking you to side with at least one of them. [spoiler]By the way, one of them is a registered sex offender. And somehow, that's not even the reason he's creepy![/spoiler] Even your interactions with the women in the cast are usually about various aforementioned creepy men. [spoiler]The closeted lesbian coming out to (she believes) the woman she has a crush on? That conversation fails the Bechdel test, even if you consider the player impersonating Anna to be a "named woman."[/spoiler] So even though it's supposed to be about Anna, it's more accurately about men fighting over a woman-shaped trophy called Anna.
It may seem like I'm kind of harping on this but that's only because so MUCH of their characterization is either behaving inappropriately towards women or being belligerent to people in general. There's not much to go on without that.

As for the narrative, it was... railroady. I didn't feel like I was finding secrets because even if I found out something a little early, one of the guys would just tell me to do it later. The highly telegraphed railroading in the intro was actually my favorite UI moment in the game, but that was a lot more artful than the clumsy dialogue trees that all lead to a single point.
I did think the big bad was interesting, especially the part about [spoiler]how "a strong individual would simulate a better [life]" rather than live fully in a suboptimal one[/spoiler]. Though I felt like that theme of [spoiler]the appearance being more meaningful than the substance[/spoiler], while present in some parts of the game, such as [spoiler]reporting a colleague for harassment being an issue because it could reflect poorly on the company, or the folder of pictures of random women that Taylor just Has, Apparently[/spoiler], was underutilized. Which is odd, because... that's from your villain monologue—you HAVE to establish those themes in the story up to that point.

There's just a lot that could have been considerably better than it was.

review_text_raw:
Sad to say that I had to refund this. The premise seemed solid based on the store page - trying to piece together clues to someone's disappearance when you only have their phone - and the general interface was well done, but that was about it. My first hour of playing this mostly consisted of:

[list]
[*] Listening to overdramatic, very slowly worded voice messages.
[*] Piecing together "corrupted" pictures and texts that had absolutely nothing to do with Anna's disappearance. 
[*] Wondering if a proofreader was ever used for this game. Most of the articles and texts gave me the impression that English isn't the developer's first language. While I have nothing against that, coming across awkward grammar really took the immersion out of a mostly text-based game.
[*] Sitting through consecutive rounds of text-vomit finger-pointing from Greg and Taylor. I truly detest people who text at a rate of 50 messages/min when a single sentence would have sufficed. I didn't think it could get any worse, but in came the relationship drama...
[*] An overall disconnect between the gameplay and the plot. A girl disappears with clear hints of some non-human entity behind it, so why am I wasting my time investigating the sorry backgrounds of two garden-variety losers?
[/list]

Maybe the game gets better beyond the 1.7-hour point, but I really didn't have the patience to sit through constant notifications from the Male MC Idiot Express while waiting for some actual horror story to happen. Honestly, I'd have been happier to just shut the damn phone off and actually set out to find Anna door to door. At least then the "investigation" would have felt more productive.

review_text_raw:
I enjoy these 'immersive sim' games where you look through devices for clues to a mystery like A Normal Lost Phone or even Hypnospace Outlaw. I liked trawling through old messages and finding tidbits of information that would help me solve a mystery or hack into a passworded account to find more clues. 

I thought that Simulacra would be similar to those kinds of games, but maybe with a more harrowing twist as it's labelled as 'horror'. However I found there to be minimal 'puzzle' elements here, and any that did exist were fairly obvious to figure out. Instead the game is pushed forward by the other characters in the game, who clearly tell you what to do next at each stage.

So the focus of the game is mainly on the story, which I felt was pretty weak. The characters kept railroading me into doing things I didn't want to, like investigating a topic I didn't think had merit, or making me give information to somebody I didn't trust in order to push the plot forward. I thought the final reveal was bizarre and the 'villain's' motives were contrived. It seemed like the devs were trying to send some fancy message about society but hadn't done a good enough job of fleshing it out throughout the game so it all just felt flat at the end.

Several of the other reviews describe the tone of the plot as 'goofy', which I think is fitting but weird for a so-called horror game. Unfortunately the horror aspects solely comes from the occasional jump scare where an image pop ups with a scream, like the prank videos people used to send each other....

And lastly, there are 4 different endings, but getting them is really unsatisfying. To get the best ending, you have to constantly lie to people even if there is seemingly no reason to do so. The middle endings rely on you going out of your way to befriend a random stranger during a potential kidnapping, despite the game giving you many reasons to suspect them. Most people will choose to remain suspicious of every potential suspect but still not lie to anyone, and get the bad ending which makes all your work a waste of time.

There are a ton of grammar mistakes in the English version that make situations unclear, and make the actions of characters within the story seem unrealistic, or come out of nowhere. review_text_raw:
The Good Stuff:

The layout and idea behind the game is pretty cool. I like how each "app" generally feels like a real app where you can do whatever, like comment of peoples posts or call random numbers. It is really neat design idea and it is well executed.

I also enjoyed a few of the more difficult puzzles, as they really added a sense of immersion into digging through someone's phone. The puzzles are mainly pretty easy, but the game doesn't baby you through them at all, so you feel smart when you manage to pull of something a bit more complicated.

The Bad Stuff:

For me, story is one of the most important parts of a game like this, and unfortunately SIMULACRA fails to deliver a good one.

Mild Spoilers: [spoiler]While the ending tried to be Black Mirror-esque, I feel like the story fails to properly set up the ending, so it kinda comes out of nowhere. Also, many things in the story aren't well explained or left to Deus Ex Machina[/spoiler]

There are multiple endings, and you will get an idea of what they all are when you finish the game. Some of the potential outcomes have me slightly curious, but not enough to replay it to see them. Perhaps the story would have been more interesting had I gotten a different ending.

I am not a huge fan of horror, but I have played games like Prey and Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice that have a creepy horror feel. The creepiness of SIMULACRA lasts only about the first 30 mins and then you become generally innoculated.

The main title song was also pretty cheesy.

As many other reviews have pointed out, some of the voice acting is on the level of "so bad it's hilarious".

I understand that with a smaller scale game like this it is difficult, but I felt like the chat options often strong-armed me into things I didn't want to say, which made things like [spoiler]gaining Taylor's trust[/spoiler] feel unfair.

The Bottom Line: If you want a game with a good story, there are better games. If you want a game where choices matter, there are better games. If you want a horror game, there are better games. If you just want to see a cool mechanic in action, then you might want to check it out.

SIMULACRA is a horror video game that has been highly anticipated by fans of the genre. However, after spending 1 hour playing the game, it has become clear to me that it falls far short of expectations.

One of the most disappointing aspects of SIMULACRA is the lack of polish in the graphics and sound design. The game is supposed to take place in the world of a smartphone, but the graphics are clunky and not at all realistic. The sound design is equally disappointing, with poorly implemented jump scares and music that doesn't fit the tone of the game.

The gameplay itself is also frustrating, with slow load times and confusing puzzles that are more frustrating than enjoyable. The story, which revolves around a missing person and the player's attempt to uncover the truth, is poorly executed and lacks the tension and scares that make a horror game truly effective.

In comparison to other horror games, SIMULACRA falls short in every aspect. The characters are one-dimensional and uninteresting, and the player's options for weapons and actions are limited. Even the in-game purchases feel like a desperate attempt to make up for the overall lack of quality in the game.

In my personal opinion, SIMULACRA is a major disappointment. It fails to deliver on the promise of an immersive horror experience and falls far short of the standard set by other games in the genre. I would not recommend this game to anyone and would give it a rating of 2/10.

Here, let me sum up this game for you: LOUD NOISES LOUD NOISES, LOUD NOISES ARE SCARY RIGHT? HORROR IS JUST LOUD NOISES RIGHT? ALRIGHT FAM REV UP THOSE EARRAPES

It seems that the developer has a complete lack of ability to write an actually scary horror story, so they decided to go for the streamerbait technique of just putting EPIC JUMPSCARES in place of, you know, any sort of actual effort. 

The worst part is that there's only 4 or 5 actual jumpscares with actual scares (spooooooky bleeding faces and whatnot), all the rest are perfectly normal things (like a call, a system message, a phone glitch)  with ridiculously loud sound effects to startle you.
